subject: High site fidelity and spatial models

messages.author: 7329857f6e47dae0
messages.subject: High site fidelity and spatial models
parts:
Hello everyone,

I’m very new to capture-recapture models in general and seeking advice from those of you with more experience.

We are monitoring cave roosting bats. We want to develop a sampling strategy and analysis framework suitable to calculate population size (or density If spatial models are suitable) as well as survival to monitor population trends in the long term.

Pilot data: Individuals have been identified from genetic profiles amplified from scat material collected under roosting sites (detectors). The pilot data was not collected with capture-recapture analysis in mind; however, important insights can be derived. As mentioned above, we are looking at implementing a better sampling strategy.

Inter-annual data: Across a four-year period 319 unique individuals have been identified and 51 individuals have been recaptured at least once across the four years.  Of these, 35% (18 ind)  were recaptured in the same roost, 37% (19 ind) recaptured in 2 different roosts and the remaining individuals were detected  in 3 to 5 roosts.

Intra-annual data: when looking at each year independently, between 56-100% of recaptures occur in the same roost.

Given the above background here are my questions:

1.)    Would a spatial method be suitable for my species? My initial thought was that they were not, because the great majority of recaptures occur in the same roost and according to the secr manual, spatial recaptures are required to derive a good estimate of D.  However, on a phidot post on another animal and extreme site fidelity, it was mentioned that setting sigma to an arbitrary number could work but caution was warranted.

Any additional thoughts? I’m thinking of going the non-spatial route.

 2.)    What about the inter-annual data? There are almost equal proportions of recaptures in a single or multiple roost. Would a spatial method be advisable?  Any warnings?

 3.)    My final question is regarding the number of recaptures. It has been mentioned that a minimum of 10-20 recaptures are required to obtain sensible results.  Do these numbers translate to a proportion of the captures? Or is it 20 individuals independently of whether you capture 500 or 50 indv.

 

Thanks heaps,

 

Diana

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: High site fidelity and spatial models
parts:
Hello Diana

I'm not sure I can help much. The spatial capture-recapture (SECR) models in the R package 'secr' apply to populations distributed more or less evenly in 2 dimensions. If your bats are clustered at a few roosts then that is not what you need. What density would you be estimating? The openCR phidot post (interesting - I had forgotten that!) was an attempt to deal with sporadic tree-specific sampling effort for a frog that (effectively) didn't move between trees, whereas your bats do move between roosts.

A non-spatial multi-state model for the discrete subpopulations is more suitable (e.g., Lebreton et al. 2009 Advances in Ecological Research 41). I'm not saying that is going to be easy, and you could just choose to ignore the spatial (roost) structure in a non-spatial analysis. You should find help on phidot from people who know MARK or E-SURGE.  If you estimate population size from a non-spatial model then do think about exactly what population you are trying to estimate (in spatial sampling N is usually not well defined).

One danger of ignoring spatial structure is that you miss the spatial component of individual heterogeneity in detection probability, and that can bias estimates of population size and survival. Whether that is an issue depends on other details like the ranging behaviour of the bats, the extent of the sampling are, the sampling protocols etc.

On your last question - yes, the 20 recaptures rule of thumb is independent of the total.

That's how it looks to me today - I hope you can elicit other opinions. Clustering is not uncommon, but usually it is seen just as a threat to variance estimates in SECR models, whereas in your case it is fundamental to the population structure and sampling.

Murray
